q: Does the Krylov + qubitization scheme's exponential-in-D convergence and its shallow D-vs-N slope survive extension to non-abelian gauge groups (SU(2), SU(3)) where link variables force a larger local Hilbert space and Gauss-law constraints become non-trivial?
basis: The paper treats only U(1) 1+1D (Schwinger). Non-abelian gauge groups introduce link-variable qubit registers (or bosonic truncations) and a much larger H_0 spectrum, which could both (a) reduce the reference-state / ground-state overlap and thus require a much larger D, and (b) worsen Hankel ill-conditioning at fixed D. Neither the paper nor this replication tests it.
next_steps: Pick a small SU(2) Kogut-Susskind lattice (e.g. N=4 sites with j_max=1/2 link truncation), build H analogous to Eq. 15 with the link-electric term, choose a physically motivated strong-coupling reference state, and re-run the same QSE-vs-D convergence sweep on a classical simulator. Compare threshold-D to the U(1) case at matched qubit count.

q: How does the paper's moment-based (Hankel) QSE compare quantitatively to modern quantum-Krylov variants (Motta et al. QLanczos, Cortes-Gray thermal Krylov, Klymko QK-eig with real-time evolution) on the same Eq. 15 instance?
basis: The paper uses one specific quantum Krylov protocol (block-encoded moments). Other quantum-Krylov variants trade different resources: QLanczos needs imaginary-time evolution, Klymko et al. use real-time Trotterized evolution with a smaller condition number, and thermal Krylov variants have different sample-complexity scaling. Their relative advantage on this specific Schwinger instance is not tested.
next_steps: Implement classically each of the three main quantum-Krylov variants on the paper's exact Eq. 15 at mu=1.5, x=0.5, N=4-10; compare (a) D at threshold 10^-4, (b) cond(S) growth, and (c) sensitivity to simulated shot noise on the matrix elements. This is pure numpy, one afternoon of work.

q: Is the block-encoding Otilde(N) gate-cost advantage over prior Otilde(N^2) LCU quantitatively confirmed when the qubitization circuit is actually compiled and T-counted (not just asymptotically bounded) for the paper's own N=10, 26, 100 target sizes?
basis: Sec. 5-6 gives an asymptotic gate-count analysis; the extrapolation to N=100, 1000, 10000 is analytical. Constants and log factors matter for crossover: a scheme that is Otilde(N) with a big prefactor can lose to Otilde(N^2) with a small one at any realistic N. This replication did not run a compiler-level resource estimate.
next_steps: Use Qualtran or Azure QRE to compile the paper's PREPARE/SELECT decomposition for Eq. 15 at N=10, 20, 50, 100; T-count the block encoding; compare against a naive LCU compilation of the same Hamiltonian. Report the crossover N and whether the asymptotic advantage is realised at practically-relevant sizes.

q: How does the Krylov step degrade under realistic hardware noise (depolarising, dephasing, shot noise on moment estimates), and specifically at what noise level does the exponential-in-D convergence collapse to polynomial or worse?
basis: The paper's Sec. 4.3 gives a shot-noise-based extrapolation but does not model gate-level noise. On real hardware the block-encoded moment estimates m_k = <psi|H^k|psi> are estimated by many shots of a possibly noisy block-encoding circuit whose error compounds with k. If gate noise dominates for k > k_max, the effective usable D is capped independently of shot count.
next_steps: Simulate noisy moment estimation on Eq. 15 at N=4-10 by adding Gaussian error to each m_k with variance from (a) shot noise only, (b) shot noise + a per-application depolarising channel with error rate 10^-3, 10^-4, 10^-5. Plot smallest achievable Delta E / E_int as a function of noise rate. Estimate the D_max(noise) and compare against the noiseless slope D(N) = 0.057 N + 4.36.

q: Can a learned / ML-driven choice of Krylov basis (adaptive-basis QSE, variational Krylov, or reinforcement-learned reference-state ansatz) reduce the required D or delay the Hankel ill-conditioning breakdown for the same Eq. 15 instance?
basis: The paper fixes the Krylov basis as powers of H applied to a fixed reference state. In classical numerical linear algebra, adaptive / restarted Krylov methods (implicitly-restarted Arnoldi, block Krylov, deflation) can dramatically reduce D for fixed accuracy. Whether an analogous adaptive strategy has a quantum-implementable analogue that beats the fixed-basis Hankel protocol on Schwinger is untested.
next_steps: Explore three heuristics classically on Eq. 15 at N=6-10: (i) restarted Krylov keeping the K best Ritz vectors, (ii) block Krylov starting from multiple orthogonal reference states, (iii) a small parametric ansatz for the reference state whose parameters are optimised by classical VQE-style outer loop before the Krylov step. Report threshold-D and cond(S) growth vs the paper's fixed-basis Hankel baseline.
